records.coreQuestion: Where does a harvest wait between the field and your bread, and why does it matter?
records.openingLine: Why 25 billion bushels wait in silos.
records.secondBeat: That's America's grain storage capacity, as of 2017.
records.dependency: Farmers, millers and exporters depend on grain elevators to store and move harvests year-round.
records.mechanism: Elevators receive grain at harvest, dry and store it, then load it onto trains, barges and ships.
records.bottleneck: Storage has consolidated into far fewer, larger elevators.
records.failureConsequence: An elevator outage at harvest leaves grain piled in fields or unsold.
records.resilience: On-farm bins and temporary piles cover some shortfalls, with spoilage risk.
records.expectedConsequence: prices at the farm gate drop when storage runs short
editorialTitles: The Silos Between the Field and Your Bread
Why Grain Storage Is a Hidden Chokepoint

facts.claim: In 2017, the United States had 0.88 cubic kilometres (25 billion US bushels) of storage capacity, a growth of 25% over the previous decade.
In 1961, 1,642 country elevators were in Alberta, holding 3,452,240 tonnes of grain.
By 2010, only 79 primary elevators remained, holding 1,613,960 tonnes.
It had a capacity of 40,000 tons and its automatic conveying and spouting system could distribute grain into 226 bins.

narration.text: Why 25 billion bushels wait in silos.
That's America's grain storage capacity, as of 2017.
Elevators hold harvests until mills and ships are ready.
In 1961, Alberta had 1,642 country elevators.
By 2010, only 79 primary elevators remained.
US storage capacity grew 25% in a decade.
Lose one at harvest, and grain has nowhere to go.
That's why a few big silos steady the price of bread.

records.topic: Why Donated Blood Expires in 42 Days
records.coreQuestion: Why can't hospitals stockpile blood, and what happens when cold storage fails?
records.openingLine: Why donated red cells expire in 42 days.
records.dependency: Surgery, trauma care and cancer treatment depend on a steady supply of stored blood components.
records.mechanism: Red cells are refrigerated, platelets kept at room temperature, and plasma frozen, each with its own shelf life.
records.bottleneck: Short shelf lives mean supply must be replenished constantly by donors.
records.failureConsequence: A refrigeration failure can force blood banks to discard stock.
records.resilience: Regional networks can ship units between hospitals.
records.expectedConsequence: elective surgeries are postponed when stocks run low
editorialTitles: Why Blood Can't Be Stockpiled
The Cold Chain Behind Every Transfusion

facts.claim: Units of whole blood and red blood cells are kept refrigerated at 1.0 to 6.0 °C, with maximum permitted storage periods of 35 and 42 days respectively.
Platelets can be stored at room temperature for up to 5–7 days.
Fresh frozen plasma can be stored at a very low temperature of −30 °C for up to 12 months.
Further extending the shelf life of stored blood up to 42 days was an anticoagulant preservative, CPDA-1, introduced in 1979.

narration.text: Why donated red cells expire in 42 days.
They're refrigerated at 1 to 6 °C.
Platelets last only 5 to 7 days at room temperature.
Plasma, frozen at −30 °C, keeps for 12 months.
A 1979 preservative stretched red-cell life to 42 days.
One failed fridge can force a hospital to discard its stock.
That's why blood supply depends on donors every single week.

records.coreQuestion: Who actually records that you own a share, and how much flows through them?
records.openingLine: Why $2.5 quadrillion flowed through one company.
records.dependency: Most U.S. securities trades settle through DTCC's depository and clearing subsidiaries.
records.mechanism: Securities are immobilised in a central depository and ownership changes by book entry.
records.bottleneck: One organisation settles the vast majority of U.S. securities transactions.
records.failureConsequence: An outage would freeze settlement across the market.
records.resilience: Backup sites and settlement cycles are designed to absorb disruptions.
records.expectedConsequence: trades would stall unsettled and margin calls would spread
editorialTitles: The Company That Settles the Stock Market
Why Your Shares Live in One Depository

facts.claim: In 2022, DTCC settled the vast majority of securities transactions in the United States and $2.50 quadrillion in value worldwide, making it by far the highest financial value processor in the world.
DTCC was established in 1999 as a holding company to combine the Depository Trust Company (DTC) and National Securities Clearing Corporation (NSCC).
Established in 1973, DTC was created to reduce costs and provide efficiencies by immobilizing securities and making book-entry changes to show ownership of the securities.
On March 3, 2022, DTCC blocked Russian securities from the Bank of Russia and The Ministry of Finance of the Russian Federation.

narration.text: Why $2.5 quadrillion flowed through one company.
That's what DTCC settled in 2022.
It settles the vast majority of U.S. securities trades.
Since 1973, shares have sat immobilised in its depository.
Ownership changes by book entry, not paper certificates.
If it stopped, trades would pile up unsettled.
That's why owning a share means trusting one ledger.

records.topic: The Batteries Buying Data Centres 15 Minutes
records.coreQuestion: What keeps servers running in the seconds after the grid fails?
records.openingLine: The grid fails. The batteries have 15 minutes.
records.secondBeat: That's typical battery runtime for an uninterruptible power supply.
records.dependency: Data centres, telecom sites and hospitals depend on UPS systems to bridge power cuts.
records.mechanism: Batteries supply power instantly while generators start or equipment shuts down safely.
records.bottleneck: Battery runtime is short, so the generator handover must work every time.
records.failureConsequence: If the UPS or the handover fails, servers drop instantly.
records.resilience: Redundant UPS modules and generators reduce single points of failure.
records.expectedConsequence: a failed handover turns a brief outage into a full crash
visualScenes: battery strings in a UPS room
editorialTitles: What Happens to Data Centres When the Grid Fails?
The Batteries Behind Every Data Centre
Why Servers Survive a Blackout

facts.claim: The on-battery run-time of most uninterruptible power sources is relatively short (typically ranging from 5 to 15 minutes) but sufficient to start a standby power source or properly shut down the protected equipment.
The switch-over time can be as long as 25 milliseconds depending on the amount of time it takes the standby UPS to detect the lost utility voltage.
Many ferroresonant UPSs are 82–88% efficient (AC/DC-AC) and offer excellent isolation.
Many systems used in telecommunications use an extra-low voltage common battery 48 V DC power.

narration.text: The grid fails. The batteries have 15 minutes.
That's typical battery runtime for an uninterruptible power supply.
It's enough to start generators or shut down safely.
Some standby units take up to 25 milliseconds to switch over.
If the generator doesn't start in time, everything drops.
Telecom sites often run on 48-volt battery plants.
That's why the internet's uptime rests on a few minutes of batteries.

records.topic: The Pipes Behind the Flint Water Crisis
records.coreQuestion: How did a change in water treatment expose a city to lead from its own pipes?
records.openingLine: Why 100,000 people drank from leaching pipes.
records.secondBeat: Flint skipped corrosion inhibitors, and old lead lines leached.
records.dependency: Cities with old lead service lines depend on corrosion control to keep lead out of tap water.
records.mechanism: Corrosion inhibitors form a protective layer inside pipes; without them, lead leaches into water.
records.bottleneck: Lead lines run to individual homes and are slow and costly to replace.
records.failureConsequence: Without corrosion control, lead exposure spreads through the network.
records.resilience: Replacement programmes remove lead lines, one street at a time.
records.expectedConsequence: residents rely on bottled water while pipes are dug up
editorialTitles: How Old Pipes Poisoned Flint's Water
Why Lead Lines Are So Hard to Replace

facts.claim: The Flint water crisis was a public health crisis from 2014 to 2019 which involved the drinking water for the city of Flint, Michigan, being contaminated with lead.
Officials failed to apply corrosion inhibitors to the water, which resulted in lead from aging pipes leaching into the water supply, exposing around 100,000 residents to elevated lead levels.
Between 6,000 and 12,000 children were exposed to drinking water with high levels of lead.
On August 20, 2020, the victims of the water crisis were awarded a combined settlement of $600 million; by November, the settlement grew to $641 million.
An extensive lead service pipe replacement effort has been underway since 2016.

narration.text: Why 100,000 people drank from leaching pipes.
Flint skipped corrosion inhibitors, and old lead lines leached.
Between 6,000 and 12,000 children were exposed.
The crisis ran from 2014 to 2019.
Settlements began at $600 million and grew to $641 million.
Replacing the lead pipes has been underway since 2016.
That's why a treatment chemical matters as much as the pipes.

records.topic: The Membranes Pushing Seawater at 82 Bar
records.coreQuestion: Why does turning seawater into drinking water take so much pressure and power?
records.openingLine: Why seawater must be pushed at 82 bar.
records.secondBeat: Reverse osmosis forces water through salt-blocking membranes.
records.dependency: Coastal cities in dry regions depend on reverse-osmosis desalination for drinking water.
records.mechanism: Pumps force seawater through membranes that let water pass and hold salt back.
records.bottleneck: Overcoming seawater's natural osmotic pressure takes high pressure and energy.
records.failureConsequence: Membrane fouling or power loss cuts water output directly.
records.resilience: Storage reservoirs and parallel trains cover short outages.
records.expectedConsequence: water supply drops as soon as the pumps stop
editorialTitles: How Seawater Becomes Drinking Water
Why Desalination Needs So Much Pressure

facts.claim: RO requires pressure between 2–17 bar (30–250 psi) for fresh and brackish water, and 40–82 bar (600–1200 psi) for seawater.
Seawater has around 27 bar (390 psi) natural osmotic pressure that must be overcome.
Seawater RO systems typically require 2.9-5.5 kWh/m3, although state-of-the-art systems are around 2.3 kWh/m3.
By 1985, rapid growth led the city to operate the world's largest low-pressure RO plant, producing 56.8 million liters per day.

narration.text: Why seawater must be pushed at 82 bar.
Reverse osmosis forces water through salt-blocking membranes.
Seawater's natural osmotic pressure is about 27 bar.
Plants run at 40 to 82 bar to beat it.
That takes 2.9 to 5.5 kilowatt-hours per cubic metre.
Cut the power, and the fresh water stops.
That's why coastal cities' water is really an energy problem.

records.topic: The 62 Million Tonnes of E-Waste a Year
records.coreQuestion: Where do the world's discarded electronics go, and how much is actually recycled?
records.openingLine: Why only 22.3% of e-waste gets recycled.
records.secondBeat: The world generated about 62 million tonnes in 2022.
records.dependency: Recovery of copper, gold and rare metals from old electronics depends on specialised smelters and collection.
records.mechanism: Collected devices are dismantled and shredded, then smelted to recover metals.
records.bottleneck: Only a fraction of e-waste is formally collected and recycled.
records.failureConsequence: Uncollected e-waste ends up in landfills or informal burning.
records.resilience: Take-back rules and urban mining can raise collection rates.
records.expectedConsequence: valuable metals are lost and toxins leak into landfills
editorialTitles: Where the World's E-Waste Goes
Why Most Old Electronics Aren't Recycled

facts.claim: In 2022, approximately 62 million tonnes of electronic waste were generated globally; only 22.3% were formally collected and recycled.
Global e-waste generation is projected to reach 82 million tonnes by 2030.
Around 70% of toxic waste in landfills is electronic waste, even though e-waste accounts for only 3% of the waste in landfills.
A 2011 report found that of 215,000 tons of electronics imported to Ghana, 30% was brand new and 70% was used.

narration.text: Why only 22.3% of e-waste gets recycled.
The world generated about 62 million tonnes in 2022.
That's projected to reach 82 million tonnes by 2030.
E-waste is 3% of landfill waste, but 70% of its toxic waste.
Smelters can recover metals only from what gets collected.
Everything else leaks value and toxins.
That's why collection, not technology, limits e-waste recycling.

records.topic: The White Pigment in Two-Thirds of Everything
records.coreQuestion: Why is one white powder in most paints, plastics and papers, and who makes it?
records.openingLine: Why China makes 6.0 of 9.9 million tonnes.
records.secondBeat: That's the world's titanium dioxide pigment capacity.
records.dependency: Paints, plastics, paper and coatings depend on titanium dioxide for whiteness and opacity.
records.mechanism: Titanium ores are processed chemically into fine TiO2 pigment particles.
records.bottleneck: China holds most of the world's pigment capacity.
records.failureConsequence: Plant outages or trade limits raise prices for paints and plastics.
records.resilience: Producers in other regions can raise output, but capacity is limited.
editorialTitles: The White Powder in Almost Everything
Why China Dominates Titanium Dioxide

facts.claim: World TiO2 pigment capacity was estimated at 9.9 million tonnes per year in 2025, of which China accounted for 6.0 million tonnes.
It has been estimated that titanium dioxide is used in two-thirds of all pigments, and pigments based on the oxide have been valued at a price of $13.2 billion.
World production in 2014 exceeded 9 million tonnes.
Rutile is the next most abundant and contains around 98% titanium dioxide in the ore.

narration.text: Why China makes 6.0 of 9.9 million tonnes.
That's the world's titanium dioxide pigment capacity.
It goes into about two-thirds of all pigments.
Those pigments are worth about $13.2 billion.
Paint, plastic and paper get their bright white from it.
Plant outages there ripple into paint prices everywhere.
That's why one white powder is a supply-chain story.

records.topic: The Chemical Made in Bigger Volumes Than Any Other
records.coreQuestion: Why is ethylene the most produced organic chemical, and what depends on it?
records.openingLine: Why 225 million tonnes of one gas matter.
records.secondBeat: No organic compound is made in greater volume.
records.dependency: Plastics, antifreeze, solvents and packaging depend on ethylene from steam crackers.
records.mechanism: Steam cracking breaks hydrocarbons into ethylene, which is converted into polymers and intermediates.
records.bottleneck: Output is concentrated in large, capital-intensive crackers.
records.failureConsequence: A cracker outage tightens supply of plastics feedstock across a region.
records.resilience: Global trade in derivatives and spare cracker capacity absorb some shocks.
editorialTitles: The Chemical Behind Most Plastics
Why Ethylene Crackers Matter So Much

facts.claim: Ethylene's worldwide production (over 225 million tonnes in 2022) exceeds that of any other organic compound.
By 2013, ethylene was produced by at least 117 companies in 32 countries.
In the United States and Europe, approximately 90% of ethylene is used to produce ethylene oxide, ethylene dichloride, ethylbenzene and polyethylene.
Ethylene is widely used in the chemical industry.

narration.text: Why 225 million tonnes of one gas matter.
No organic compound is made in greater volume.
About 90% becomes polyethylene and a few key chemicals.
By 2013, 117 companies in 32 countries made it.
It comes from giant steam crackers that take years to build.
One outage can tighten plastic supply for a whole region.
That's why so much packaging traces back to one molecule.

records.topic: The Circles Draining America's Biggest Aquifer
records.coreQuestion: Why do the Great Plains look like green circles, and what water feeds them?
records.openingLine: Why one aquifer needs 6,000 years to refill.
records.secondBeat: The Ogallala feeds the Great Plains' crop circles.
records.dependency: Much of U.S. irrigated farming depends on groundwater from the Ogallala Aquifer.
records.mechanism: Center-pivot sprinklers rotate around a well, watering circular fields.
records.bottleneck: The aquifer refills far more slowly than farms pump it.
records.failureConsequence: As water tables fall, wells run dry and fields revert to dryland farming.
records.resilience: Efficiency upgrades and crop switching slow depletion.
records.expectedConsequence: farm output drops where wells fail
visualScenes: aerial view of green crop circles
Ogallala Aquifer map across eight states
editorialTitles: The Aquifer Behind America's Crop Circles
Why the Ogallala Can't Refill in Time

facts.claim: It underlies an area of approximately 174,000 sq mi (450,000 km2) in portions of eight states.
About 27% of the irrigated land in the entire United States lies over the aquifer, which yields about 30% of the ground water used for irrigation in the United States.
Since 1950, agricultural irrigation has reduced the saturated volume of the aquifer by an estimated 9%.
Once depleted, the aquifer will take over 6,000 years to replenish naturally through rainfall.
Center-pivot irrigation was invented in 1940 by the farmer Frank Zybach, who lived in Strasburg, Colorado.

narration.text: Why one aquifer needs 6,000 years to refill.
The Ogallala feeds the Great Plains' crop circles.
It supplies about 30% of America's irrigation groundwater.
Center-pivot sprinklers, invented in 1940, pump it up.
Since 1950, irrigation has drained an estimated 9% of it.
Where wells run dry, farms fall back to rain alone.
That's why those green circles are borrowing ancient water.

records.topic: The 500 Million Pallets Moving Europe's Goods
records.coreQuestion: Why does Europe's freight sit on one standard wooden pallet?
records.openingLine: Why 500 million pallets share one size.
records.secondBeat: European railways standardised the EUR-pallet in 1961.
records.dependency: Warehouses, trucks and retailers depend on interchangeable standard pallets.
records.mechanism: A shared pallet standard lets loads move between companies without restacking.
records.bottleneck: Pallet supply and repair must keep pace with freight volumes.
records.failureConsequence: A pallet shortage slows loading and raises costs across supply chains.
records.resilience: Pooling companies and repair networks recycle pallets continuously.
records.expectedConsequence: loading slows and pallet prices spike
editorialTitles: The Wooden Standard Behind Europe's Freight
Why One Pallet Size Rules Logistics

facts.claim: Around 450-500 million EUR-pallets are in circulation.
The weight of a EUR/EPAL-pallet (EPAL 1) is approximately 25 kg.
The safe working load of a EUR/EPAL-pallet is 1,500 kg.
The maximum additional load can be up to 4,000 kg when stacking.
In 1961 the European railways commissioned the standardization of a common pallet type under the auspices of the UIC.

narration.text: Why 500 million pallets share one size.
European railways standardised the EUR-pallet in 1961.
Each weighs about 25 kilograms.
It safely carries 1,500 kilograms.
Stacked, it can bear up to 4,000 kilograms more.
Around 450 to 500 million are in circulation.
When pallets run short, loading docks slow down.
That's why a wooden standard keeps Europe's freight moving.

records.topic: The Network Approving 257.5 Billion Card Payments
records.coreQuestion: What happens in the seconds between tapping your card and the approval beep?
records.openingLine: Why 257.5 billion payments ran through one network.
records.dependency: Merchants and cardholders worldwide depend on card networks to authorise payments in real time.
records.mechanism: Each payment request travels from the merchant to the card network to the issuing bank and back for approval.
records.bottleneck: A few networks carry most card transactions.
records.failureConsequence: An outage stops card payments at shops across countries at once.
records.resilience: Offline limits, redundant data centres and other networks absorb some disruptions.
records.expectedConsequence: shoppers switch to cash or abandon purchases
editorialTitles: What Happens When You Tap Your Card
The Network Behind Billions of Payments

facts.claim: In 2025, Visa's global network (known as VisaNet) processed 257.5 billion transactions worth US$14.2 trillion.
By 1972, licenses had been granted in 15 countries.
Visa sold 406 million shares at US$44 per share, raising US$17.9 billion in what was then the largest initial public offering in U.S. history.
During the late 1960s, BofA also licensed the BankAmericard program to banks in several other countries.

narration.text: Why 257.5 billion payments ran through one network.
That's VisaNet's transaction count for 2025.
Those payments were worth $14.2 trillion.
Each tap travels to the network, then the bank, then back.
All of it happens in the seconds before the beep.
An outage stops card payments in shops across countries.
That's why cash registers depend on a few data centres.

records.coreQuestion: How did $1 trillion in market value disappear and return in about half an hour?
records.secondBeat: It was the flash crash of May 6, 2010.
records.dependency: Investors depend on exchange matching engines and liquidity providers to trade at fair prices.
records.mechanism: Matching engines pair buy and sell orders in microseconds; algorithms supply much of the liquidity.
records.bottleneck: When algorithms pull back at once, liquidity can vanish instantly.
records.failureConsequence: Prices can plunge far below fair value in minutes.
records.resilience: Circuit breakers now pause trading during extreme moves.
records.expectedConsequence: orders fill at absurd prices before the market recovers
visualScenes: stock index plunging on a screen
editorialTitles: The Day $1 Trillion Vanished in Minutes
What the 2010 Flash Crash Revealed

facts.claim: The flash crash of May 6, 2010 was a United States trillion-dollar flash crash; temporarily, $1 trillion in market value disappeared.
The crash lasted for approximately 36 minutes.
It was also the second-largest intraday point swing up to that point, at 1,010.14 points.
Twenty minutes later, by 3:07 p.m., the market had regained most of the 600-point drop.

narration.text: Why $1 trillion vanished in 36 minutes.
It was the flash crash of May 6, 2010.
The market swung 1,010.14 points in a day.
Most of the 600-point drop came back within minutes.
Matching engines pair orders, but algorithms supply the liquidity.
When they pulled back together, prices fell through the floor.
That's why markets now have circuit breakers built in.

records.topic: The Ransomware That Turned Away NHS Patients
records.coreQuestion: How did one piece of ransomware force hospitals to divert ambulances?
records.openingLine: Why ransomware diverted British ambulances in 2017.
records.secondBeat: WannaCry hit more than 300,000 computers in 150 countries.
records.dependency: Hospitals depend on networked computers for records, imaging, scheduling and admissions.
records.mechanism: Clinical systems share data across a hospital network; malware can spread across the same network.
records.bottleneck: Old, unpatched systems left many trusts exposed.
records.failureConsequence: When systems lock up, hospitals divert patients and cancel care.
records.resilience: Paper fallbacks and network segmentation limit the damage.
records.expectedConsequence: ambulances divert and appointments are cancelled
visualScenes: ransom screen on a hospital PC
worm spreading across a network diagram
editorialTitles: When Ransomware Hit Britain's Hospitals
Why Hospital IT Is Critical Infrastructure

facts.claim: The attack was estimated to have affected more than 300,000 computers across 150 countries, with total damages ranging from hundreds of millions to billions of dollars.
On 12 May, some NHS services had to turn away non-critical emergencies, and some ambulances were diverted.
In 2016, thousands of computers in 42 separate NHS trusts in England were reported to be still running Windows XP.
In 2018 a report by Members of Parliament concluded that all 200 NHS hospitals or other organisations checked in the wake of the WannaCry attack still failed cybersecurity checks.

narration.text: Why ransomware diverted British ambulances in 2017.
WannaCry hit more than 300,000 computers in 150 countries.
Some NHS services turned away non-critical emergencies.
In 2016, 42 NHS trusts still ran Windows XP machines.
A year later, all 200 organisations checked still failed security reviews.
When records and scans lock up, care slows immediately.
That's why hospital IT is as critical as its oxygen supply.

records.topic: The Three Digits That Took 30 Years to Reach Everyone
records.coreQuestion: Why did it take decades for 911 to reach almost every American?
records.secondBeat: The first 911 system went live in 1968.
records.dependency: Emergency response depends on a universal number routing calls to local dispatch centres.
records.mechanism: Calls to 911 are routed to a public safety answering point that dispatches police, fire or ambulance.
records.bottleneck: Each local area had to build its own answering and routing infrastructure.
records.failureConsequence: Where 911 is down, callers can't reach help through the usual number.
records.resilience: Backup centres and text-to-911 add redundancy.
records.expectedConsequence: response slows when routing or dispatch centres fail
editorialTitles: How 911 Reached Almost Everyone
The Slow Rollout of America's Emergency Number

facts.claim: AT&T made its first implementation in Huntington, Indiana on March 1, 1968.
Regarding national US coverage, by 1979, 26% of the US population could dial the number.
This increased to 50% by 1987 and 93% by 2000.
As of March 2022, 98.9% of the US population has access.
As of 2008, each year Canadians make twelve million calls to 911.

narration.text: Why 911 reached only 26% by 1979.
The first 911 system went live in 1968.
Each area had to build its own answering centre.
Coverage hit 50% by 1987 and 93% by 2000.
By 2022, 98.9% of Americans had access.
When a centre goes down, calls must reroute fast.
That's why three simple digits sit on a patchwork of local systems.

records.coreQuestion: Why did one COVID-19 vaccine need freezers colder than Antarctica?
records.secondBeat: It shipped in containers held at −80 to −60 °C.
records.dependency: mRNA vaccine distribution depended on ultra-low-temperature freezers and shipping containers.
records.mechanism: The vaccine was shipped in special containers holding −80 to −60 °C, then thawed for use.
records.bottleneck: Many countries' cold chains handle only 2 to 8 °C.
records.failureConsequence: Without ultra-cold storage, doses spoil before reaching patients.
records.resilience: Dry-ice shippers and later formulations eased storage requirements.

The Cold Chain Behind mRNA Vaccines

facts.claim: During distribution the vaccine is stored in special containers that maintain temperatures between −80 and −60 °C (−112 and −76 °F).
India's existing cold chain network can handle only temperatures between 2 and 8 °C (36 and 46 °F), far above the requirements of the vaccine.
In February 2021, Pfizer revealed that the entire sequence initially took about 110 days on average from start to finish.
Initial guidance recommended a two-dose regimen, given 21 days apart.

narration.text: Why one vaccine needed −80 °C freezers.
It shipped in containers held at −80 to −60 °C.
India's cold chain handled only 2 to 8 °C.
Making each batch took about 110 days start to finish.
Without ultra-cold storage, doses spoil on the way.
So rollout was fastest where freezers already existed.
That's why a freezer can decide how fast a vaccine reaches people.
